specPoints.text: understand how factors may increase the risk of developing coronary heart disease

primer.text: The heart feeds itself first: coronary arteries wrap it, delivering the oxygen and glucose its muscle burns every second. When fatty plaque narrows those arteries, chest pain and heart attacks follow. This note links diet, blood pressure and smoking to the plumbing failure.

lessons.title: Coronary Arteries Under Attack
lessons.opening: Coronary heart disease begins when fatty plaque, built largely from cholesterol, narrows the arteries supplying the cardiac muscle, restricting flow so the muscle runs short of oxygen.
keyPoints: Coronary arteries supply cardiac muscle with oxygen and glucose.
Plaque deposits build mainly from cholesterol.
Dietary cholesterol arrives from animal products.
The liver also synthesises cholesterol into the blood.
Partial blockage causes angina; complete blockage causes a heart attack.

low.restatement: Fatty layers narrow the heart's own supply lines; partial narrowing aches, total blockage kills muscle.
low.analogy: A kettle's element furring with limescale until it overheats and fails.
low.examPointer: Keep angina (partial) and heart attack (complete) strictly separate in answers.

medium.restatement: Narrowed lumens cut the flow, so the muscle beyond cannot respire aerobically; the blockage's completeness decides pain versus infarction.
medium.analogy: A garden hose kinked slightly versus shut off entirely — trickle versus drought.
medium.examPointer: Name the muscle's need as oxygen for aerobic respiration when explaining the damage.

check.stem: What do the coronary arteries supply?

options.text: The cardiac muscle with oxygen and glucose
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Pulmonary vessels serve the lungs.
Brain supply runs via the carotid arteries.
Renal vessels serve the kidneys; urea is a waste, not a supply.

check.stem: What mainly forms the fatty deposits in coronary heart disease?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Water hardness is not the named culprit.
Sugar is not the plaque material cited.
Cells do not build the plaques.

check.stem: Which symptom follows PARTIAL blockage of a coronary artery?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
A heart attack needs complete blockage.
Partial narrowing already causes pain on exertion.
Coughing is not the coronary symptom here.

check.stem: Why does complete blockage cause a heart attack?

options.text: The muscle beyond receives no oxygen, so aerobic respiration stops and cells die
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Because the blood pressure falls to zero everywhere
options.explanation: The blockage is local, not systemic.

options.text: Because the plaque poisons the muscle
options.explanation: The damage is oxygen starvation, not poison.

options.text: Because the heart stops pumping entirely
options.explanation: Other regions may keep contracting; the starved region fails.

check.stem: From which two sources does the body's cholesterol come?

options.text: Animal products in the diet and synthesis by the liver
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Neither is a cholesterol source.
Neither builds cholesterol.
Neither organ manufactures dietary cholesterol.

check.modelAnswer: It is the build-up of fatty plaque inside the coronary arteries, restricting the flow that supplies cardiac muscle.

check.stem: State what happens to the lumen as plaque builds up.
check.modelAnswer: The lumen narrows and blood flow through the artery is reduced.

check.stem: Explain why the heart muscle is especially vulnerable to blocked arteries.
check.modelAnswer: Because it contracts constantly and depends on aerobic respiration, so any interruption of its oxygen and glucose supply quickly starves the tissue it serves.

check.stem: A patient reports chest pain only when climbing stairs. Suggest the coronary explanation.
check.modelAnswer: Effort raises the muscle's oxygen demand, so a partially narrowed coronary artery cannot keep up, and the shortfall produces angina during exertion.

lessons.title: The Risk Factors Behind the Plaques
sourceHeadings: Risk factors of coronary heart disease
lessons.opening: Obesity, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and smoking each raise the odds of coronary heart disease — the first by straining the heart, the second by damaging vessel walls, and the last two by feeding and accelerating the plaques.
keyPoints: Obesity strains the heart and can lead to Type 2 diabetes.
High blood pressure damages the artery walls.
High cholesterol speeds plaque build-up toward blockage.
Smoking chemicals raise plaque growth and blood pressure.
Carbon monoxide in smoke cuts the blood's oxygen carriage.

low.restatement: Too much weight, pressure, cholesterol or smoke all push the same disease forward.
low.analogy: Four ways to overload a bridge: heavier trucks, faster traffic, worn cables, missing inspections.
low.examPointer: List all four factors when a question says 'risk factors'; two or three alone lose marks.

medium.restatement: The factors converge on the same endpoint — narrowed coronary lumens — through strain, wall damage, faster deposits and reduced oxygen carriage.
medium.analogy: Four tributaries feeding one flood: different routes, same river.
medium.examPointer: For smoking, name BOTH mechanisms: plaque plus pressure, and carbon monoxide's grip on red cells.

check.stem: How does obesity raise coronary risk?

options.text: Extra weight strains the heart and can cause Type 2 diabetes, which damages vessels
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Obesity adds oxygen to the blood
options.explanation: It does not; it multiplies demand.
If anything, diet-linked cholesterol rises.
Thinning is not the mechanism; damage comes via diabetes and strain.

check.stem: What does high blood pressure do to the vessels?

options.text: The increased force against the walls damages them
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Damage narrows function rather than widening.
Pressure and rate are separate properties.
Pressure does not scour plaques.

check.stem: Which component of smoke reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of red blood cells?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Nicotine drives plaque and pressure, not the oxygen grip.
Tar coats airways rather than red cells.
Exhaled gas is not the smoke component cited.

check.stem: How does smoking accelerate plaque build-up?

options.text: Chemicals in smoke increase both plaque growth and blood pressure
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
It does the opposite.
Thinning is not the named effect.
The coronary link is explicit here.

check.stem: Which risk factor speeds the deposits toward blockage most directly?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Pressure damages walls; cholesterol is the plaque material.
Obesity acts indirectly through strain and diabetes.
Sleep is not among the named four.

check.stem: List the four risk factors named for coronary heart disease.
check.modelAnswer: Obesity, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and smoking.

check.stem: Name the diabetes type linked to increased weight in this context.
check.modelAnswer: Type 2 diabetes can follow increased weight and further damages blood vessels.

check.stem: Explain why several different risk factors end in the same disease.
check.modelAnswer: Because each one pushes toward the same physical outcome — narrowed coronary arteries — whether through strain, wall damage, faster deposits or poorer oxygen carriage.

check.stem: A smoker switches to a low-cholesterol diet. Which risk remains and why?
check.modelAnswer: Smoking remains a risk, because its chemicals still raise blood pressure and plaque growth while carbon monoxide still cuts the oxygen carriage of the red cells.

glossary.definition: The vessels wrapping the heart and supplying its muscle.
The fatty deposit, mainly cholesterol, narrowing arterial lumens.
Chest pain caused by partial coronary blockage during exertion.
A smoke gas that binds red cells and cuts oxygen carriage.
